title: How Circumcision Works
summary: Josh and Chuck examine circumcision, opening with a news hook about Lloyd Schofield's proposed San Francisco referendum to ban male circumcision of minors. They cover U.S. circumcision rate trends, the anatomy of the foreskin (prepuce, frenulum, glans) and its functions, medical problems such as phimosis, paraphimosis, and balanoposthitis, religious and historical origins (Judaism, Islam, ancient Egypt, Mayans and Aztecs, the 19th-century medicalization in the West), global practice, surgical procedures and devices (Gomco clamp, Mogen clamp, plastic bell), arguments for and against circumcision including HIV and HPV claims, foreskin restoration methods, and female genital mutilation. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about missing and extra fingers.

entities.name: Journal of the American Medical Association

segments.title: Opening banter and Lloyd Schofield's proposed ban
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode with banter, then discuss Lloyd Schofield's proposed San Francisco referendum that would make circumcising a person under eighteen a misdemeanor, and the reactions to it.

segments.title: Circumcision rates and statistics
segments.summary: Statistics on U.S. circumcision: about 3 in 5 American males over the last thirty years were circumcised, falling to about 53 percent by 2005 and 33 percent by 2009, with regional differences and roughly 1.2 million circumcisions per year and about $240 million in costs.

segments.title: Anatomy of the foreskin
segments.summary: Definition of circumcision as removal of the prepuce (foreskin). The hosts describe the foreskin's covering of the glans, the frenulum, its moist inner lining, its nerve endings and blood vessels, and its protective and sensory functions.

segments.title: Foreskin problems: phimosis, paraphimosis, and smegma
segments.summary: Possible problems with the foreskin: smegma buildup from poor hygiene, phimosis when the foreskin is too tight, paraphimosis when it is too loose, balanoposthitis, and a too-short frenulum. The hosts note these problems are rare and that circumcision is rarely medically necessary.

segments.title: Origins and religious history of circumcision
segments.summary: Biblical covenant between God and Abraham, with circumcision by the eighth day for Isaac's descendants and Ishmael, the link to Judaism and Islam, and the Qur'an's lack of explicit mention. Also covers ancient Egyptians, Mayans, Aztecs, Colchians, and Christian and other faiths' stances.

segments.title: Medicalization and global practice
segments.summary: Circumcision became medicalized in the West in the nineteenth century, with claims it treated disease. Barbers in medieval Turkey performed it. Practice varies around the world, including age at circumcision, rites of passage, risks in remote African areas, and rising adoption in South Korea and the Philippines.

segments.title: Circumcision procedures and devices
segments.summary: Description of infant circumcision with restraint and anesthesia, the Gomco clamp, the plastic bell device, and recovery over a few days. Also adult circumcision, which involves pulling the foreskin forward, incisions, and stitching, with a few weeks without sex.

segments.title: Arguments for circumcision
segments.summary: Reasons parents choose circumcision: religion and culture, wanting a son to match the father, fitting in with peers, claimed reductions in HPV, chlamydia, syphilis, and heterosexual female-to-male HIV transmission, and perceived cleanliness and appearance. The hosts note the study claims and caveats.

segments.title: Arguments against circumcision and foreskin restoration
segments.summary: Arguments against circumcision: it is mutilation, unnecessary per the American Academy of Pediatrics, carries risks of scarring and infection, removes a child's right to choose, reduces sensitivity, and may cause psychological effects. Methods to restore a foreskin (skin grafts, stretching with weights and straps, balloon inflation) are described. Terminology preferences (natural, intact) are noted.
topics: American Academy of Pediatrics circumcision policy

segments.title: Female genital mutilation and closing remarks
segments.summary: Comparison with female genital mutilation, including clitoridectomy and infibulation, its historical Western practice, the WHO and UN response, and the hosts' comparison to male circumcision before closing with a pointer to the HowStuffWorks article.

segments.title: Listener mail: missing and extra fingers
segments.summary: Listener stories about fingers lost in accidents, a prosthetic finger, polydactyly with extra pinkies removed at birth, and a factory accident where fingers were pinched off and reattached.
